questions.question: What is dynamic programming and when do you use it?
questions.title: Dynamic Programming Introduction Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Dynamic programming (DP)** solves problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems and caching results to avoid recomputation. Use it when a problem has **optimal substructure** (optimal solution is built from optimal sub-solutions) and **overlapping subproblems** (same subproblems appear repeatedly).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can identify when DP applies and explain the two key properties
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Applying DP to problems that don't have overlapping subproblems — DP is overkill for simple divide-and-conquer
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain both top-down (memoization) and bottom-up (tabulation) and when you'd choose each

sections.title: Cache Overlapping Subproblems
sections.content: Two required properties: (1) **Optimal substructure**: the optimal solution to the whole problem can be constructed from optimal solutions to subproblems. (2) **Overlapping subproblems**: the naive recursive solution solves the same subproblems multiple times. DP stores subproblem solutions in a table (**bottom-up/tabulation**) or cache (**top-down/memoization**) so each subproblem is solved exactly once. Classic DP problems: fibonacci, longest common subsequence, 0/1 knapsack, coin change, edit distance.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Two conditions: optimal substructure + overlapping subproblems
- Top-down (memoization): recursive + cache (HashMap or array)
- Bottom-up (tabulation): iterative + fill table from base cases
- Bottom-up: no recursion overhead, often O(1) space with optimization
- Top-down: more intuitive, only computes needed subproblems
- If no overlapping subproblems: divide-and-conquer (merge sort) not DP
- Identify DP: 'count ways', 'maximum/minimum value', 'is it possible'

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Dynamic programming applies when two properties hold: the problem has optimal substructure — meaning the optimal solution is built from optimal sub-solutions — and overlapping subproblems — the same subproblems appear multiple times in a naive recursive solution. DP caches those subproblem results to avoid recomputing them. Top-down memoization adds caching to the recursive solution, while bottom-up tabulation builds from base cases iteratively. I recognize DP problems by phrases like 'count the number of ways', 'find the minimum cost', or 'is it possible' — these often indicate optimal substructure over a sequence or grid.

questions.question: How do you solve the coin change problem using dynamic programming?
questions.title: Coin Change DP Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Bottom-up DP: create dp[amount+1] initialized to infinity. dp[0] = 0.** For each amount from 1 to target, try each coin — if coin <= amount, `dp[amount] = min(dp[amount], dp[amount-coin] + 1)`. Return dp[target] (or -1 if still infinity). O(amount × coins) time.

interviewer_intent.testing: Classic unbounded knapsack DP — tests ability to formulate the recurrence and initialize correctly
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Initializing dp array to 0 instead of a large value (Integer.MAX_VALUE or amount+1), or forgetting the dp[0]=0 base case
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the recurrence relation clearly: dp[i] = min over all coins c where c <= i of (dp[i-c] + 1)

sections.title: Bottom-Up Tabulation
sections.content: `dp[i]` = minimum coins to make amount `i`. **Base case**: `dp[0] = 0`. **Fill**: for each `i` from 1 to amount: for each coin `c`: if `c <= i` and `dp[i-c] != Integer.MAX_VALUE`: `dp[i] = Math.min(dp[i], dp[i-c] + 1)`. **Answer**: `dp[amount]` — if still Integer.MAX_VALUE, return -1 (impossible). **Recurrence**: `dp[i] = min(dp[i-c] + 1) for all coins c <= i`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- dp[i]: minimum coins to make amount i
- Initialize dp[0]=0, dp[1..amount]=Integer.MAX_VALUE or amount+1
- Recurrence: dp[i] = min(dp[i-c]+1) for each valid coin c
- Outer loop: amounts 1 to target
- Inner loop: all coins
- Check dp[i-c] != MAX before adding 1 (avoid overflow)
- Time: O(amount × n_coins), Space: O(amount)
- Top-down version: memo[amount] with recursion

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I use bottom-up DP. I create a dp array of size amount plus one, initialized to infinity — meaning we don't yet know how to make those amounts — with dp zero set to zero as the base case. Then I fill the table from 1 to the target amount. For each amount I try each coin: if the coin value doesn't exceed the current amount and the sub-problem dp of amount minus coin is reachable, I update dp of this amount to the minimum of its current value and dp of amount minus coin plus one. The recurrence is: minimum coins for amount i equals one plus the minimum coins for amount i minus any valid coin. The final answer is dp at the target amount.

followup_questions: How do you count the number of ways to make change?
What is the difference between coin change I and coin change II?

questions.question: What is the longest common subsequence (LCS) problem?
questions.title: Longest Common Subsequence LCS Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **LCS** finds the length of the longest subsequence common to two strings (not necessarily contiguous). Use a 2D DP table: `dp[i][j]` = LCS of `s1[0..i-1]` and `s2[0..j-1]`. If characters match, `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1`; else `max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])`. O(m×n) time and space.

interviewer_intent.testing: 2D DP formulation — one of the most commonly asked DP problems in interviews
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing LCS with the longest common substring (which must be contiguous — different problem)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the recurrence clearly, note that LCS is the basis for diff tools and DNA sequence alignment

sections.title: 2D DP Table
sections.content: `dp[i][j]` = length of LCS of `s1[0..i-1]` and `s2[0..j-1]`. **Base cases**: `dp[0][j] = dp[i][0] = 0` (empty string has LCS 0). **Fill**: if `s1.charAt(i-1) == s2.charAt(j-1)`: `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1`. Else: `dp[i][j] = Math.max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])`. Answer: `dp[m][n]`. **LCS vs Substring**: subsequence = not contiguous (can skip); substring = must be contiguous.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Subsequence: characters in order but not necessarily adjacent
- Substring: characters must be adjacent (contiguous)
- LCS recurrence: match → diagonal+1; mismatch → max(up, left)
- Table size: (m+1) × (n+1) with 0-row and 0-column for base cases
- Time: O(m×n), Space: O(m×n) or O(min(m,n)) with row optimization
- LCS length is the answer; to reconstruct, trace back through the table
- Applications: diff tool (git diff), DNA alignment, spell checker

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: LCS finds the longest sequence of characters that appear in the same order in both strings, but not necessarily contiguous. I build a 2D DP table where dp[i][j] represents the LCS length for the first i characters of string one and first j characters of string two. If the characters match, I extend the diagonal cell by one. If they don't match, I take the max of ignoring the current character of either string — looking up or left in the table. The answer is in the bottom-right cell. I'd distinguish LCS from the longest common substring, which requires contiguous characters and uses a different recurrence.

questions.question: How do you solve the 0/1 knapsack problem using dynamic programming?
questions.title: 01 Knapsack Problem DP Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **0/1 knapsack**: given items with weights and values, maximize value with a weight capacity. `dp[i][w]` = max value using first i items with capacity w. For each item: either skip it (`dp[i-1][w]`) or include it (`dp[i-1][w-weight[i]] + value[i]`). Take the max. O(n×W) time and space.

interviewer_intent.testing: The foundational DP problem — tests whether you can formulate the include/exclude recurrence
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing 0/1 knapsack (each item once) with unbounded knapsack (items can be reused)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the 1D space optimization where you use a single dp array but iterate weight backwards

sections.title: Include or Exclude Each Item
sections.content: `dp[i][w]` = max value using items 1..i with capacity w. For item i with weight `wt[i]` and value `val[i]`: if `wt[i] > w`: cannot include — `dp[i][w] = dp[i-1][w]`. Else: `dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], dp[i-1][w-wt[i]] + val[i])`. Answer: `dp[n][W]`. **1D optimization**: use `dp[W]` and iterate weight backwards from W to wt[i] to avoid using the same item twice.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- 0/1: each item used at most once
- Recurrence: max(exclude, include) = max(dp[i-1][w], dp[i-1][w-wt]+val)
- Table: (n+1) × (W+1)
- 1D optimization: iterate weight backwards → O(W) space
- Unbounded knapsack: iterate weight forwards (items can be reused)
- Time: O(n×W), Space: O(n×W) or O(W) optimized
- Coin change is unbounded knapsack variant

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The 0/1 knapsack asks for maximum value given weight capacity where each item can be used at most once. I build a 2D DP table where dp[i][w] represents the max value using the first i items with weight limit w. For each item I have two choices: skip it, carrying forward dp[i-1][w], or include it if its weight fits, giving dp[i-1][w minus its weight] plus its value. I take the max. The 1D space optimization uses a single array and iterates the weight dimension backwards — this prevents an item from being counted twice since we're referencing the previous row's values in reverse.

questions.question: How do you solve the 0/1 knapsack problem with DP?
questions.title: 0/1 Knapsack Problem: Bottom-Up DP Solution
questions.direct_answer: Define dp[i][w] as the maximum value using the first i items with capacity w; for each item either skip it or take it if it fits, choose the maximum, and fill the 2D table bottom-up.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can define a DP state, write the recurrence relation, and implement a 2D bottom-up table
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing the state definition or forgetting to check that the item weight does not exceed the current capacity before taking it
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Clearly articulate the state, the transition, the base case, and mention the O(n*W) space optimisation to a 1D array

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
I always start by defining the DP state. dp[i][w] represents the maximum value achievable using the first i items when the knapsack capacity is exactly w. The answer we want is dp[n][W] where n is the number of items and W is the total capacity.

The base cases are: dp[0][w] equals zero for all w, because with zero items we earn nothing; and dp[i][0] equals zero for all i, because with zero capacity we can carry nothing.

The recurrence for each item i and capacity w has two choices. First, skip item i: the value is dp[i-1][w] — same as the best we could do with the previous items. Second, take item i, but only if weight[i] is less than or equal to w: the value is dp[i-1][w - weight[i]] plus value[i]. We take the maximum of the two choices.

We fill the table row by row, left to right. The final answer is in dp[n][W].

Time complexity is O(n times W) and space is also O(n times W) for the 2D table. If the interviewer asks for optimisation, I can reduce space to O(W) by keeping only the current and previous rows, or even a single 1D array traversed right to left.

I always mention that 0/1 knapsack is the canonical DP problem because it demonstrates state definition, recurrence, and table filling in the clearest way possible.

sections.title: Key Points
content: State: dp[i][w] = max value with first i items and capacity w
Recurrence: dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], dp[i-1][w-weight[i]] + value[i]) if weight[i] <= w
Base cases: dp[0][w] = 0 and dp[i][0] = 0 for all i, w
O(n*W) time and space; optimise to O(W) with a 1D array traversed right to left
Demonstrates the three DP pillars: state definition, recurrence, bottom-up filling

followup_questions: How does the 0/1 knapsack differ from the unbounded knapsack problem?
How do you reconstruct which items were selected, not just the maximum value?

questions.question: What is memoization vs tabulation in DP and which should you use in interviews?
questions.title: Memoization vs Tabulation in Dynamic Programming
questions.direct_answer: Memoization is top-down recursion with a cache; tabulation is bottom-up iteration filling a table — both have the same time complexity, but in interviews start with memoization since it is easier to derive, then convert to tabulation if asked to optimise.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand both DP implementation styles and can explain the trade-offs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating memoization and tabulation as having different time complexities — they solve the same subproblems and are asymptotically identical
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that memoization also incurs call-stack overhead (O(n) extra space) that tabulation avoids, and give a concrete interview strategy

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
Memoization and tabulation are two ways to implement dynamic programming, and understanding both distinguishes a prepared candidate.

Memoization is the top-down approach. You write the natural recursive solution, then add a HashMap or array to cache the result of each subproblem the first time it is computed. On subsequent calls with the same input you return the cached result immediately. The benefit is that it is easy to derive from a recursive solution — you are essentially adding two lines: a cache lookup at the start and a cache store before returning. The downside is that it still uses O(n) call-stack space on top of the cache space.

Tabulation is the bottom-up approach. You identify the base cases, fill them into a table, then iteratively compute each subsequent entry using previously filled entries. There is no recursion, so no call-stack overhead. For large inputs this avoids the StackOverflowError risk entirely.

Both approaches compute the same subproblems and have identical time complexity — O(n) for Fibonacci, O(n times W) for knapsack, and so on.

My interview strategy is to start with memoization because it is faster to write and easier to verify on a whiteboard or shared editor. I mention upfront: 'I will start with top-down memoization because it is more natural to derive; I can convert to bottom-up tabulation if you want the iterative version.' Interviewers appreciate this transparency.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Memoization: top-down recursion + cache (HashMap or array); natural to derive from recursion
Tabulation: bottom-up iterative table-filling; no call-stack overhead
Both have the same time complexity — they solve the same subproblems
Memoization uses O(n) extra stack space; tabulation does not
Interview strategy: start with memoization, offer to convert to tabulation if asked
